items.cite: Macdonald, Hugh. *Bizet*. New York: Oxford University Press, 2014.
items.note: The starting point for understanding how a prize-winning pianist spent his adult life trying to establish himself in the theatre. Read alongside Macdonald’s online catalogue when a familiar title conceals an unfinished project or a later editor’s intervention.

items.cite: McClary, Susan. *Georges Bizet: Carmen*. Cambridge Opera Handbooks. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1992.
items.note: For the question the tunes alone cannot answer: how does the opera make gender, class and its imagined Spain audible? Places the score beside Mérimée’s novella, its reception and later adaptations; especially useful before returning to the final duet.

items.cite: Curtiss, Mina. *Bizet and His World*. New York: Alfred A. Knopf, 1958.
items.note: For the people and working conditions behind the operas: letters, family relationships, publishers and Parisian theatres. Its documentary abundance remains valuable, while dates and claims about musical versions should be compared with newer scholarship.

items.cite: Bizet, Georges. *Lettres à un ami, 1865–1872*. Edited by Edmond Galabert. Paris: Calmann-Lévy, 1909.
items.note: For Bizet speaking about composition and the practical frustrations of a career before Carmen. This is an edited, posthumously published correspondence, not a diary or an unmediated account of every event.

items.cite: Macdonald, Hugh. *The Bizet Catalogue*. Washington University in St Louis. Online thematic catalogue.
items.note: For checking what Bizet actually wrote: composition dates, manuscripts, early editions, letters, premières and later alterations. The Carmen and L’Arlésienne entries are particularly helpful in separating the composer’s work from recitatives, suites and revisions made after his death.
